newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers tighten roadblocks; budget vote due.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers tighten roadblocks; budget vote due.

text.p: Defiant Greek farmers tightened a 23-day road blockade on Saturday which has cut the country's main north-south highway, inflicting Christmas transport woes and heavy economic damage.

The farmers in the Thessaly region, heartland of the revolt, clamped down on any trucks trying to pass a succession of barricades after the socialist government again refused to meet their economic demands.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis, whose belt-tightening 1997 budget will be voted in parliament on Saturday night, has told the farmers that the government has no more money to give.
He has refused to meet the farmers personally until they lift their barricades but he has also ruled out using force to expell the farmers from the national roads.
His hardline stand paid off in the northern Macedonia and Thrace regions on Friday, where farmers decided to lift their blockades and to meet with Simitis in Athens on Monday.
But the Thessaly farmers, who began the revolt, said they would not cave in and that they would again stop all traffic trying to pass the blockades made up of thousands of tractors.

The Thessaly farmers had been letting through an increasing number of cars and lorries to try to win over public sympathy. Farmers also kept up blockades on the Egeion road, cutting off the western port of Patras which services traffic with Italy.
"We are tightening the blockades. Simitis can't even be bothered to meet us. He is counting on dividing us but it won't work," said Yannis Pattakis, a farmers' leader in Larissa.
The tightening of the blockades is expected to cause misery for Greeks trying to leave Athens over the weekend to return to their villages for Christmas holidays, police said.
Police federations appealed to the government and farmers on Friday to find a solution before the Christmas period when many of Athens' four million residents want to return to villages.
Socialist officials said that Simitis was hoping to convince some of the Thessaly farmers to abandon their barricades and to join his talks with Macedonian and Thracian farmers on Monday.
Simitis, elected on pledged of economic reform in September, has also been heartened by a decison by seamen on Friday to call off a five-day strike.
The seaman had shut ports around Greece, leaving trucks stranded and tourists furious. Fistfights had erupted between truckers, seamen and police.

An array of strikes and work disruptions has swept Greece in the run-up to the 1997 budget vote at midnight on Saturday. Damages from the farmers' blockades alone have been put at more than $100 million.
Farmers want cheaper fuel, higher price supports and $1.3 billion in debts rescheduled.
Simitis's 1997 austerity budget is expected to pass easily through the 300-seat parliament, where he has a solid absolute majority.
He has said the budget and accompanying biting tax reforms are essential if Greece is to meet European Union targets for a single currency. Greece hopes to join a single currency by 2001.

The budget and a tax reform bill cut public hiring, clamp down on pension increases and sweep away previous tax breaks. They also impose new or higher taxes on everything from alcohol and cigarettes to the first tax on interest from state bonds.
